title: Design exercise: chat and presence
summary: A classic design exercise: real-time messaging with groups, history, receipts and presence at millions of concurrent connections. The reference answer separates connection gateways from conversation ownership, orders each conversation through a single owner chosen by consistent hashing, partitions history by conversation and time bucket, batches fan-out per gateway, keeps presence best effort and off the message path.

exercise.prompt: Design a messaging service: one-to-one and group conversations, delivered in real time to connected devices, with history that users can scroll back through, delivery and read receipts, and a presence indicator that shows who is online.

constraints.caption: Constraints and numbers.
rows: Send a message to a conversation (up to 1,000 members, assumption); deliver it to every connected member in order; store history forever; page through history.
Delivered and read receipts; online, away and offline presence.
50 million daily active users; 5 million concurrent connections at peak; 1 billion messages per day.
An average message of 200 bytes of text, about 500 bytes stored with metadata; a user reads about 20 messages for every one sent.
derive the per-second rates, the connection count per gateway and the storage growth yourself
Delivery to a connected member within 500 ms at p99 inside one region; history page under 100 ms at p99.
99.95 percent availability for sending and delivery; messages are never lost once the sender sees the acknowledgement.
End-to-end encryption, voice and video, media storage (a media reference is a URL to an object store), spam and abuse detection, search ranking.

clarifying_questions.a: A total order per conversation: every member sees the same sequence. No ordering across conversations.
At least once to the device, deduplicated by message id on the client; the server acknowledges to the sender only after the message is durable.
Up to 1,000 members. Larger broadcast channels are a different product and out of scope.
Yes: a user may have several sessions; each gets every message, and read receipts are per user, not per device.

Online within a few seconds of connecting; offline within 60 s of the last heartbeat (assumption); away is reported by the client when the user is idle, not inferred from heartbeats. Presence is best effort and never blocks a message.
One region per user's home; cross-region conversations route through the conversation's home region. The reference answer is single-region.

blocks.text: Every number below follows from the stated assumptions: 50 million daily active users, 5 million concurrent connections, a billion messages a day of 500 stored bytes each, and a peak at three times the daily average. The tables carry the arithmetic; the paragraphs carry the assumptions.

blocks.caption: Rates and daily volumes derived from the assumptions.

20 reads per send; mostly the newest messages of a conversation, which is what the partition layout must serve cheaply
5 million connections, one small frame every 30 s each (assumption)

blocks.caption: Sizes: the message store and the gateway fleet.
rows: 500 GB times 365; rules out one database node and makes partitioning the first decision
assumption; a connection costs tens of kilobytes of memory and a heartbeat every 30 s
5 million connections divided by 50,000, plus headroom for a zone loss: 150 nodes in three zones
a few round trips of 500 microseconds
the latency reference numbers; the 500 ms p99 target is generous and exists to absorb queueing under load

blocks.text: Two of these numbers decide the shape of the design. The storage growth says history must be partitioned from day one, and partitioned so that a page of recent messages is one bounded read. The delivery rate says fan-out must be batched: a message to a thousand members cannot cost a thousand network sends.

Clients hold one WebSocket (RFC 6455: upgrade handshake, framing, ping and pong, close) to a stateless-enough gateway that knows only which sessions it holds. Conversations are owned by conversation servers chosen by consistent hashing of the conversation id, so one server orders all writes of a conversation. The conversation server persists the message, assigns its position, and fans it out to the gateways that hold the members' sessions. Offline members get a push notification from an event consumer; a search indexer consumes the same events.

Each arrow says how the call is made: TLS from clients, TCP through the load balancer s7, RPC and batched deliveries between tasks by IP address, named SDK calls over the DynamoDB gateway endpoint s8 and the Kinesis interface endpoint s9, cache reads and writes with a TTL s10. Sync means the caller waits for the answer; async means the work goes on after the caller has been answered. The gateway fleet is drawn twice, as the sender's gateway on the way in and as the members' gateways on the way out, so that the diagram has no cycle. Gateways learn the conversation servers' task addresses from ECS service discovery s11 and hash conversation ids over that list. The VPC frames are one VPC in one Region across three Availability Zones.

blocks.text: Presence and the session registry are plain keys with a TTL, so a gateway that dies cleans up after itself: its sessions expire within the TTL and its clients reconnect to another gateway. The balancer needs no rule for that, because a new connection simply lands on a task that is healthy.

blocks.text: The condition on the sort key costs nothing extra and does one thing: if two conversation servers ever believe they own a conversation after a failover, the second write of a message id fails instead of replacing the first. Deduplication of a retried send is the owner's job: its in-memory tail holds the recent client_msg_ids and is rebuilt from the table when the conversation moves, so no second item per message is written. The ack is sent only after DynamoDB answers 200, which is the neutral design's rule that the sender hears nothing before the message is durable.

blocks.caption: WebSocket termination: a Network Load Balancer with Fargate gateways, an Application Load Balancer, or the API Gateway WebSocket API.

rows.option: Network Load Balancer, TLS listener, in front of Fargate gateway tasks
rows.pick_when: the connections are long-lived and numerous, the application speaks its own protocol over a WebSocket, and certificates should be managed by the balancer
rows.avoid_when: the capacity-unit charge for millions of TLS connections would be the largest line
rows.example: For this design: chosen. This is the neutral L4 balancer: it passes the connection to a task that holds it. The price is the capacity unit: a TLS unit holds 3,000 active connections, so the 5 million sessions come to about $7,320 a month, about 70 percent of the gateway tasks' bill.

rows.option: Network Load Balancer, TCP listener, TLS terminated in the gateways
rows.pick_when: the connection count is high enough that the TLS capacity unit dominates, and the team can deliver certificates to the tasks and spend their CPU on encryption
rows.avoid_when: nobody wants to manage certificates on tasks, or the encryption CPU is not available
rows.example: For this design: the first lever, not the first choice. A TCP unit holds 100,000 active connections, so the same sessions would cost about $290, set by the bytes processed (300 bytes a delivered frame, assumption), not by the connection count; the price is encryption work on 150 tasks and a certificate to distribute.

rows.option: Application Load Balancer in front of Fargate tasks
rows.pick_when: the entry needs HTTP routing by path or host, authentication actions, or one balancer for the WebSocket and the history API
rows.avoid_when: the traffic is long-lived connections, because a capacity unit holds 3,000 active connections a minute
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. It supports WebSockets natively, but the neutral design asks for a plain L4 hop, and the unit holds the same 3,000 connections as the TLS unit of the network balancer at a higher price per unit-hour.

rows.pick_when: the backend is functions, connections are few or short, and per-connection routing, authorisation and throttling are worth a per-message price
rows.avoid_when: connections must last more than 2 hours, or the backend pushes millions of messages a minute to connections
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. A connection ends after 10 idle minutes or at 2 hours, a push is one POST to the connection's callback address with no batching per gateway, and the delivery rate of 175,000 a second is far above the default quota of 10,000 requests a second for the whole account.

blocks.caption: The message store: DynamoDB, Amazon Keyspaces, or Aurora.

rows.option: Amazon DynamoDB, on-demand, the Standard-IA table class
rows.pick_when: access is by one partition key and a sort key range, writes are many and small, history is kept and rarely read, and nobody wants to run a ring
rows.avoid_when: the hot path needs joins or secondary queries across conversations, or reads dominate the bill
rows.example: For this design: chosen. The key is the conversation and the bucket, the sort key the message id, so a page of history or a resync is one bounded Query. One key is limited to 1,000 write units and 3,000 read units a second by its partition, far above one conversation's rate, and the owner's in-memory tail takes the hot reads. Storage is the larger charge, which is what Standard-IA is for: about $18,000 a month for storage against $23,400 for writes.

rows.option: Amazon DynamoDB, the Standard table class
rows.pick_when: throughput is the dominant cost: little data, many requests
rows.avoid_when: storage is the dominant cost, as for a history that is kept for ever
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Its storage is $0.25 per GB-month against $0.10 for Standard-IA, so the history would cost about $63,800 a month in all instead of about $41,400.

rows.pick_when: the team already writes CQL against Cassandra, or the schema is a wide-row design it wants to keep as it is
rows.avoid_when: there is no Cassandra estate to carry over, because DynamoDB offers the same partition and sort key model
rows.example: For this design: the neutral design's layout in its original home, the Cassandra model Discord's write-ups describe. Not chosen: nothing here depends on CQL, and its on-demand prices are the same as DynamoDB Standard's ($0.625 per million writes, $0.25 per GB-month) with no cheaper storage class for a history this size.

rows.option: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, partitioned by conversation
rows.pick_when: the product needs relational queries across conversations and the data fits one cluster
rows.avoid_when: the data outgrows one cluster volume, whose limit is 128 TiB
rows.example: For this design: ruled out by size. A year of history is about 180 TB, past one cluster volume, and sharding it across clusters would be the work DynamoDB does itself.

blocks.caption: Presence and the session registry: ElastiCache for Valkey, or DynamoDB with a TTL.

rows.option: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey, node-based, a replica per shard
rows.pick_when: values are small, writes are very frequent, entries must expire within a minute, and the data can be rebuilt
rows.avoid_when: the data is the system of record and must survive a node loss without a rebuild
rows.example: For this design: chosen, as two clusters. Heartbeats are 170,000 writes a second to each cluster, each key expires by its own TTL, and a lost node costs a minute of wrong presence, not a message. The sixteen small nodes cost about $2,050 a month.

rows.option: Amazon DynamoDB with a TTL attribute
rows.pick_when: writes are modest, the items live for days, and one more store to run is the cost to avoid
rows.avoid_when: entries must expire within a minute, or the write rate is in the hundreds of thousands a second
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. A TTL delete may come days after the expiry, so every reader would filter on the timestamp itself, and 170,000 writes a second at $0.625 per million writes would be about $270,000 a month.

blocks.caption: The message events: Kinesis Data Streams, SNS with SQS, or MSK.

rows.option: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, provisioned shards, the conversation id as the partition key
rows.pick_when: the rate is high and steady enough to size, two or more consumers read the same events at their own pace, and order per key matters
rows.avoid_when: the rate is small or swings widely, or one consumer needs per-message retries
rows.example: For this design: chosen. The events are the neutral design's log: 35,000 a second at the peak, read by the push service and the indexer, each with its own position. A shard takes 1,000 records a second, so 40 shards cover the peak, and the price lists put that at about $860 a month, a fifth of on-demand mode.

rows.option: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, on-demand mode
rows.pick_when: the rate is unknown or spiky and nobody wants to size shards
rows.avoid_when: the volume is high and steady, since data written and read is billed per GB, each record rounded up to 1 KB
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Every event is billed as at least 1 KB and each of the two consumers pays for the data it reads, which comes to about $4,610 a month, about five times the provisioned stream.

rows.option: Amazon SNS in front of one SQS queue per consumer
rows.pick_when: each consumer needs its own queue, retries and dead-letter queue, and the volume is modest
rows.avoid_when: the volume is in the tens of billions of events a month, because every publish is billed
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. It would give each consumer its own queue, but 30 billion publishes a month at $0.50 per million come to about $15,000 before any queue request is paid, and with standard queues and topics the order per conversation is lost.

rows.pick_when: the team already runs Kafka, or needs its ecosystem and retention beyond what a stream offers
rows.avoid_when: there is no Kafka estate: brokers to size, patch and keep balanced
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Nothing here needs Kafka's protocol, and a stream without brokers to run does the same job.

blocks.caption: The compute: Fargate, ECS on EC2, EKS or Lambda.

rows.pick_when: steady, container-shaped services that hold connections and in-memory state, and no cluster to patch
rows.avoid_when: the platform needs kernel tuning or denser packing than a task offers, or the team runs Kubernetes for everything
rows.example: For this design: chosen for gateways, conversation servers, the push service and the indexer, on Arm tasks across three Availability Zones. A gateway holds 50,000 connections, which fits the default open-file limit of 65,535 on Fargate; the limit can be raised for headroom. The 150 gateway tasks cost about $10,200 a month.

rows.pick_when: control of the instance matters: kernel and network tuning, one very large host for many connections, or a price per connection below Fargate's
rows.avoid_when: nobody wants to patch, scale and replace instances
rows.example: For this design: the first alternative to try if the gateway line has to fall. Not chosen at the start: it adds the instances to run, and the numbers here do not need what Fargate cannot give.

rows.pick_when: the organisation already runs Kubernetes and needs its ecosystem or portability across clouds
rows.avoid_when: a handful of services and no Kubernetes estate; the cluster fee and the upgrade cadence buy nothing
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Nothing here needs the Kubernetes API, and a cluster brings three major releases a year to track for five services.

rows.pick_when: short, stateless, bursty requests with no connection to hold
rows.avoid_when: the process must hold a connection or in-memory state, or run longer than the function limit of 900 seconds
rows.example: For this design: ruled out for the connection path. A gateway holds a session for hours, the load balancer rejects a WebSocket upgrade to a function, and a conversation server keeps the tail of its conversations in memory.

blocks.title: The partition layout: why the bucket exists
items: The partition key is (conversation_id, bucket) with a time-ordered message id as the clustering key, so a page of recent history is a range scan inside one partition.
Discord's public write-up chose a bucket of about 10 days so that even the busiest conversations keep a partition under about 100 MB.
Without the bucket, a years-old conversation becomes one unbounded hot partition, which is the failure Discord's write-up describes.

reference_answer.title: The core flow, step by step

blocks.text: Sending one message to a group, from the sender's frame to the members' screens. The step numbers run on across the three parts.
Part a: the sender's gateway accepts the frame, the owning conversation server orders and persists it, and only then is the sender acknowledged.

blocks.text: The bottleneck is fan-out in large groups and the hot partition behind a busy conversation. The store sees one write per message regardless of members, but the reads of a popular conversation all land on one partition.

blocks.title: Fan-out in a 1,000-member group
items: One message is up to 1,000 deliveries.
The members' sessions sit on at most 150 gateways, so batching by gateway turns the 1,000 deliveries into at most 150 sends.
Each gateway then writes the frame to its own sessions locally, which costs no network round trip.

blocks.text: Discord's trillions-of-messages write-up reports that a hot partition frequently affected latency across their entire database cluster, and that a data service layer with request coalescing (one database read for many identical concurrent requests, routed by conversation id with consistent hashing) was the fix, alongside the database move that took their historical-message p99 from 40 to 125 ms down to 15 ms. The answer adopts coalescing in the conversation server: it already owns the conversation, so it serves recent history from an in-memory tail of the last few hundred messages and hits the store only on a miss.

Presence is the other volume problem: a user with 500 contacts coming online would notify 500 sessions, and heartbeats arrive at 170,000 per second. The design keeps presence best effort: status lives in a TTL store written by the gateway on connect, disconnect and every heartbeat; changes are fanned out only to contacts who are currently viewing that user (subscriptions held by the gateway), and status transitions are debounced so a flapping connection does not storm.

L1: Connection gateways separate from conversation ownership, with a message store partitioned by conversation.
Durable write before the acknowledgement, idempotent sends by client message id, and delivery receipts as a cursor per member.
The storage estimate (500 GB per day) and the gateway count derived from the stated assumptions.
L2: Group fan-out batched by gateway, and the hot-partition problem handled with time buckets and request coalescing.
Ordering per conversation by a single owner, with the failover behaviour stated.
History paging by range scan inside a bucket, and the reconnect resync from the last seen message id.
Presence as best effort with TTL, subscriptions and debounce, never on the message path.
L3: Multi-region sessions with a home region per conversation and the latency that costs.
The consequences of end-to-end encryption for search and server-side features.
Explicit backpressure to slow clients, and the cell layout that bounds a store outage.

interview_frame.title: A 45-minute interview
items: 0:00 to 0:05: Requirements: ordering, delivery guarantee, group size, multi-device, presence freshness, regions. Say the numbers aloud: 35,000 messages per second at peak, 175,000 deliveries per second, 5 million connections on about 100 gateways, 500 GB of history per day.
0:05 to 0:10: Entities and API: Conversation, Message with the (conversation, bucket) partition key, Receipt as a cursor, Session, Presence; the send and ack frames; the history endpoint.

0:10 to 0:20: High-level design with the diagram: gateways hold connections, conversation servers hold order by consistent hashing, the store is partitioned by conversation and time bucket, push and search consume an event log.

0:20 to 0:40: Two deep dives: the send path (durable write before ack, single-owner ordering, batched fan-out per gateway, resync on reconnect), then hot conversations and presence (bucketed partitions, in-memory tail with coalescing, best-effort presence with subscriptions).

0:40 to 0:45: Failure modes from the table, the 10x plan (regions, cells, storage tiers, backpressure), and the L3 sentence: the hard part is not sending a message, it is deciding who owns the order and what happens to that owner when it dies.
Context and scope: The current client platforms, the existing push and identity services, the ordering and loss incidents that motivate the design.
Goals and non-goals: Total order per conversation, no loss after ack, 500 ms delivery p99, 100 ms history p99; encryption, media, voice and abuse detection out of scope.
Design: This answer fills it: the gateway and conversation server split, the partition layout, the send path, presence.
Alternatives considered: Order by store clock or by a consensus log per conversation, long polling instead of WebSocket, receipts per message, with the trade-off table.

Cross-cutting concerns: Observability (delivery latency per hop, fan-out batch size, hot-partition read latency, reconnect rate), privacy of message bodies and retention, cost per connection and per stored message, rollout by conversation cohort.
Review questions the doc must answer: What a member sees in the seconds after a conversation server dies, and how a client proves it has not missed a message after a reconnect.

depth_notes.L3: Multi-region sessions, end-to-end encryption consequences for search, backpressure to slow clients.
